claim: Vaccines induce memory B-cells that provide high affinity secondary antibody responses to identical antigens.
source: Vaccines induce memory B-cells that provide high affinity secondary antibody responses to identical antigens.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about vaccine-induced immunity.

claim: Memory B-cells can re-instigate affinity maturation.
source: Memory B-cells can also re-instigate affinity maturation, but how this happens against antigenic variants is poorly understood despite its potential impact on driving broadly protective immunity against pathogens such as Influenza and Dengue.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about memory B-cell function.

claim: How memory B-cells re-instigate affinity maturation against antigenic variants is poorly understood.
source: Memory B-cells can also re-instigate affinity maturation, but how this happens against antigenic variants is poorly understood despite its potential impact on driving broadly protective immunity against pathogens such as Influenza and Dengue.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Variant protein boosts induced GCs with a higher proportion of IgM+ B cells compared to homotypic boosts.
source: Variant protein boosts induced GCs with a higher proportion of IgM+ B cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most variant protein (E4) re-stimulated GCs with the highest proportion of IgM+ cells.
source: The most variant protein re-stimulated GCs with the highest proportion of IgM+ cells with the most diverse, least mutated V-genes and with a slower but efficient serum antibody response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The most variant protein (E4) re-stimulated GCs with the most diverse V-genes.
source: The most variant protein re-stimulated GCs with the highest proportion of IgM+ cells with the most diverse, least mutated V-genes and with a slower but efficient serum antibody response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The most variant protein (E4) re-stimulated GCs with the least mutated V-genes.
source: The most variant protein re-stimulated GCs with the highest proportion of IgM+ cells with the most diverse, least mutated V-genes and with a slower but efficient serum antibody response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The most variant protein (E4) induced a slower but efficient serum antibody response.
source: The most variant protein re-stimulated GCs with the highest proportion of IgM+ cells with the most diverse, least mutated V-genes and with a slower but efficient serum antibody response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Recombinant antibodies from GC B-cells after E4 boost showed a higher affinity for the variant antigen than antibodies from a primary response.
source: Recombinant antibodies from GC B-cells showed a higher affinity for the variant antigen than antibodies from a primary response, confirming a memory origin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Higher affinity of recombinant antibodies from E4 boost GC B-cells compared to primary response confirms a memory origin.
source: Recombinant antibodies from GC B-cells showed a higher affinity for the variant antigen than antibodies from a primary response, confirming a memory origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing antibody affinities.

claim: IgM memory cells with fewer mutations participate in secondary responses to variant antigens.
source: This reveals a new process of antibody memory, that IgM memory cells with fewer mutations participate in secondary responses to variant antigens, demonstrating how the hierarchical structure of B-cell memory is used and indicating the potential and limits of cross-reactive antibody based immunity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing IgM+ GC B-cells with fewer mutations after variant boosts.

claim: Antibody-based immunity is underpinned by memory B-cells that have undergone antibody somatic hyper-mutation (SHM) and selection for improved antigen binding in germinal centres (GCs) (MacLennan et al., 1997).
source: Antibody-based immunity is underpinned by memory B-cells that have undergone antibody somatic hyper-mutation (SHM) and selection for improved antigen binding in germinal centres (GCs) (MacLennan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacLennan et al., 1997.

claim: Re-challenge with the same antigen stimulates a rapid, higher affinity, secondary antibody response.
source: Re-challenge with the same antigen stimulates a rapid, higher affinity, secondary antibody response.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about secondary immune responses.

claim: Protective immunity to highly mutable viruses, like Dengue and Influenza, can be induced by vaccination but the high level of variation often leads to immune escape (Nabel and Fauci, 2010).
source: Protective immunity to highly mutable viruses, like Dengue and Influenza, can be induced by vaccination but the high level of variation often leads to immune escape (Nabel and Fauci, 2010), leading to a focus on generating vaccine responses against conserved antigenic regions (Wu et al., 2010; Corti et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nabel and Fauci, 2010.

claim: High level of variation in viruses like Dengue and Influenza leads to a focus on generating vaccine responses against conserved antigenic regions (Wu et al., 2010; Corti et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015).
source: Protective immunity to highly mutable viruses, like Dengue and Influenza, can be induced by vaccination but the high level of variation often leads to immune escape (Nabel and Fauci, 2010), leading to a focus on generating vaccine responses against conserved antigenic regions (Wu et al., 2010; Corti et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2010; Corti et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Memory B-cells of IgM and IgG isotypes can re-instigate GCs after secondary exposure (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011; McHeyzer-Williams et al., 2015).
source: Memory B-cells of IgM and IgG isotypes can also re-instigate GCs after secondary exposure (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011; McHeyzer-Williams et al., 2015), but how this happens against variant antigens is poorly understood despite its potential impact on driving the most broadly protective immunity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011; McHeyzer-Williams et al., 2015.

claim: Memory B-cell populations show diversity, with cells expressing IgM or IgG (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011).
source: Several studies suggest diversity in the memory B-cell population, showing that cells can express IgM or IgG (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011), be mutated or non-mutated (Kaji et al., 2012) and have low affinities (Smith et al., 1997), but still persist in GCs (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011.

claim: Memory B-cells can be mutated or non-mutated (Kaji et al., 2012).
source: Several studies suggest diversity in the memory B-cell population, showing that cells can express IgM or IgG (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011), be mutated or non-mutated (Kaji et al., 2012) and have low affinities (Smith et al., 1997), but still persist in GCs (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaji et al., 2012.

claim: Memory B-cells can have low affinities (Smith et al., 1997).
source: Several studies suggest diversity in the memory B-cell population, showing that cells can express IgM or IgG (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011), be mutated or non-mutated (Kaji et al., 2012) and have low affinities (Smith et al., 1997), but still persist in GCs (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 1997.

claim: Memory B-cells can persist in GCs (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
source: Several studies suggest diversity in the memory B-cell population, showing that cells can express IgM or IgG (Dogan et al., 2009; Pape et al., 2011), be mutated or non-mutated (Kaji et al., 2012) and have low affinities (Smith et al., 1997), but still persist in GCs (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuraoka et al., 2016.

claim: Memory B-cell diversity may facilitate the recognition of antigenic variants (Herzenberg et al., 1980; Pape et al., 2011; Kaji et al., 2012).
source: It has long been speculated that this diversity may facilitate the recognition of antigenic variants (Herzenberg et al., 1980; Pape et al., 2011; Kaji et al., 2012) which could stimulate secondary GCs derived from less mutated, naïve-like, memory B-cells that still had an advantage over naive B-cells due to their increased numbers, pre-selected V-genes and lower activation thresholds (Good and Tangye, 2007; Good et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herzenberg et al., 1980; Pape et al., 2011; Kaji et al., 2012.

claim: Less mutated, naïve-like memory B-cells have advantages over naive B-cells due to their increased numbers, pre-selected V-genes and lower activation thresholds (Good and Tangye, 2007; Good et al., 2009).
source: It has long been speculated that this diversity may facilitate the recognition of antigenic variants (Herzenberg et al., 1980; Pape et al., 2011; Kaji et al., 2012) which could stimulate secondary GCs derived from less mutated, naïve-like, memory B-cells that still had an advantage over naive B-cells due to their increased numbers, pre-selected V-genes and lower activation thresholds (Good and Tangye, 2007; Good et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Good and Tangye, 2007; Good et al., 2009.

claim: Dengue-3 envelope protein (E3) was used for all priming immunisations.
source: We chose Dengue-3 envelope protein (E3) for all priming immunisations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Boost immunisations were performed 38 days after priming with identical E3 protein or variant E2 or E4 proteins.
source: Boost immunisations were performed 38 days later with identical E3 protein or variant E2 or E4 proteins which have 68% and 63% overall sequence identity with E3, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: E2 protein has 68% overall sequence identity with E3.
source: Boost immunisations were performed 38 days later with identical E3 protein or variant E2 or E4 proteins which have 68% and 63% overall sequence identity with E3, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about protein sequence identity.

claim: E4 protein has 63% overall sequence identity with E3.
source: Boost immunisations were performed 38 days later with identical E3 protein or variant E2 or E4 proteins which have 68% and 63% overall sequence identity with E3, respectively.
evidence: This is a factual statement about protein sequence identity.

claim: The cross reactivity of E3-primed mouse serum IgG correlated with sequence identity.
source: The cross reactivity of E3-primed mouse serum IgG correlated with sequence identity (Figure 1A), and overall cross-reactivity also correlated (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Overall cross-reactivity of E3-primed serum correlated with sequence identity.
source: The cross reactivity of E3-primed mouse serum IgG correlated with sequence identity (Figure 1A), and overall cross-reactivity also correlated (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Boosting with homotypic E3 antigen induced a rapid antibody memory response with anti-E3 titres rising rapidly to day 7.
source: Boosting with homotypic E3 antigen induced a rapid antibody memory response with anti-E3 titres rising rapidly to day 7, and not increasing further (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Anti-E3 titres after homotypic E3 boost did not increase beyond day 7.
source: Boosting with homotypic E3 antigen induced a rapid antibody memory response with anti-E3 titres rising rapidly to day 7, and not increasing further (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: E-protein boosted antisera was not reactive with an irrelevant His-tagged protein (PR8 HA).
source: E-protein boosted antisera was not reactive with an irrelevant His-tagged protein (PR8 HA)(Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Heterotypic boosting with E2 induced a rapid and significant increase in anti-E3 titre.
source: Heterotypic boosting with E2 induced a rapid and significant increase in anti-E3 titre, as might be expected if cross-reactive memory antibodies against the priming E3 antigen were recalled (Figure 1D), that did not increase further by day 17.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Anti-E3 titre after E2 boost did not increase beyond day 7.
source: Heterotypic boosting with E2 induced a rapid and significant increase in anti-E3 titre, as might be expected if cross-reactive memory antibodies against the priming E3 antigen were recalled (Figure 1D), that did not increase further by day 17.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: E4 boosting induced a modest but not statistically significant increase in the anti-E3 titre.
source: E4 boosting induced a modest but not statistically significant increase in the anti-E3 titre, even by day 17, showing the E4 variant boost had not induced a significant anti-E3 antibody memory response, or the induced antibodies had a low affinity for E3 (see discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The anti-E2 titre induced by the E2 boost increased about 120-fold by day 7.
source: The anti-E2 titre induced by the E2 boost increased about 120-fold by day 7 (Figure 1E), and did not increase further by day 17, further indicating that E2 boosting induced a rapid memory-like serum IgG response against E2 derived from cross-reactive E3 primed memory B-cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Anti-E2 titre after E2 boost did not increase beyond day 7.
source: The anti-E2 titre induced by the E2 boost increased about 120-fold by day 7 (Figure 1E), and did not increase further by day 17, further indicating that E2 boosting induced a rapid memory-like serum IgG response against E2 derived from cross-reactive E3 primed memory B-cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: E2 boosting induced a rapid memory-like serum IgG response against E2 derived from cross-reactive E3 primed memory B-cells.
source: The anti-E2 titre induced by the E2 boost increased about 120-fold by day 7 (Figure 1E), and did not increase further by day 17, further indicating that E2 boosting induced a rapid memory-like serum IgG response against E2 derived from cross-reactive E3 primed memory B-cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid kinetics and magnitude of the response.

claim: The anti-E4 titre induced by E4 boosting rose significantly but to a lower level, about 20-fold, by day 7.
source: Conversely the anti-E4 titre, induced by E4 boosting, rose significantly but to a lower level, about 20-fold, by day 7 (Figure 1F) and showed a further rise by day 17.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The anti-E4 titre after E4 boost showed a further rise by day 17.
source: Conversely the anti-E4 titre, induced by E4 boosting, rose significantly but to a lower level, about 20-fold, by day 7 (Figure 1F) and showed a further rise by day 17.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A boost alone did not induce a detectable antibody titre.
source: A boost alone did not induce a detectable antibody titre however, ('BO', Figure 1D) suggesting a role for memory B-cells of some type and/or cross-reactive T-cell memory, facilitating the E4 boost response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: E3 and E2 boosting induced early GC B-cell levels similarly by day 7, to 4.5–5.5% of total lymphocytes.
source: E3 and E2 boosting induced early GC B-cell levels similarly by day 7, to 4.5–5.5% of total lymphocytes, which then reduced by two-thirds by day 17 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GC B-cell levels after E3 and E2 boosting reduced by two-thirds by day 17.
source: E3 and E2 boosting induced early GC B-cell levels similarly by day 7, to 4.5–5.5% of total lymphocytes, which then reduced by two-thirds by day 17 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: E4 boosting induced GC B-cell levels about a third as high as E3 and E2 boosting.
source: E4 boosting induced GC B-cell levels about a third as high, which then reduced similarly by about 60% at day 17, remaining 4-fold higher than controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GC B-cell levels after E4 boosting reduced by about 60% at day 17.
source: E4 boosting induced GC B-cell levels about a third as high, which then reduced similarly by about 60% at day 17, remaining 4-fold higher than controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GC B-cell levels after E4 boosting at day 17 remained 4-fold higher than controls.
source: E4 boosting induced GC B-cell levels about a third as high, which then reduced similarly by about 60% at day 17, remaining 4-fold higher than controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells at day 7 after boosting correlated with increasingly variant challenge.
source: Analysis of the proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells showed a highly significant trend at day 7 after boosting, with the proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells correlating with increasingly variant challenge (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The trend of increasing IgM+ GC B-cells with variant challenge continued to day 17.
source: This trend continued to day 17.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The proportion of IgM+ B cells was consistent between individuals in an experimental group.
source: The proportion of IgM+ B cells was also consistent between individuals in an experimental group (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Overall levels of VH mutations increased in all groups from day 7 to day 17.
source: Overall levels of VH mutations increased in all groups from day 7 to day 17 (Figure 2E), consistent with secondary affinity maturation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increasing VH mutations from day 7 to day 17 is consistent with secondary affinity maturation.
source: Overall levels of VH mutations increased in all groups from day 7 to day 17 (Figure 2E), consistent with secondary affinity maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in mutations over time.

claim: There were lower levels of SHM in IgM+ GC B-cells 7 days after the variant boosts, particularly with E4, compared to the homotypic E3 boost.
source: There were lower levels of SHM in IgM+ GC B-cells 7 days after the variant boosts, particularly with the most variant protein E4, compared to the homotypic E3 boost (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Boosting with variant proteins induced early GCs with increased proportions of IgM B-cells that had fewer VH mutations.
source: Boosting with variant proteins, therefore, induced early GCs with increased proportions of IgM B-cells that had fewer VH mutations.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental data from Figures 2C and 2F.

claim: Almost every VH sequence from GC B-cells after E-protein boosts was from a distinct B-cell clone.
source: Analysis of the VH clonality of GC B-cells after E-protein boosts showed that almost every VH sequence was from a distinct B-cell clone (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The two variant boosts (E2 and E4) elicited different repertoires of VH.
source: These data also showed that the two variant boosts elicited different repertoires of VH.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 40% of the VH sequences sampled at day 7 from E2 boosted mice were either VH14-3 or the closely related VH14-4.
source: 40% of the VH sequences sampled at day 7 from E2 boosted mice were either VH14-3 or the closely related VH14-4 (black dots, Figure 2G), suggestive of a secondary response more focused on a particular epitope (see discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The prevalence of VH14-3 or VH14-4 in E2 boosted mice is suggestive of a secondary response more focused on a particular epitope.
source: 40% of the VH sequences sampled at day 7 from E2 boosted mice were either VH14-3 or the closely related VH14-4 (black dots, Figure 2G), suggestive of a secondary response more focused on a particular epitope (see discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed clonal restriction.

claim: Some VH14-3 or VH14-4 sequences were present in the homotypic E3 boost day 7 samples.
source: Some of these VH were also present in the homotypic E3 boost day 7 samples, but neither were detected at day 7 after E4 boosting (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: VH14-3 and VH14-4 were not detected at day 7 after E4 boosting.
source: Some of these VH were also present in the homotypic E3 boost day 7 samples, but neither were detected at day 7 after E4 boosting (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: E2-variant boosting induced an immediate and significant increase in avidity by day 7.
source: E2-variant boosting induced an immediate and significant increase in avidity by day 7 (Figure 3A) which did not detectably change until perhaps day 32, although data variability is high.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Avidity after E2 boost did not detectably change from day 7 until perhaps day 32.
source: E2-variant boosting induced an immediate and significant increase in avidity by day 7 (Figure 3A) which did not detectably change until perhaps day 32, although data variability is high.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A modest but significant increase in serum affinity after E2 boost was detected by day 17.
source: A modest but significant increase in serum affinity, however, was detected by day 17, with a further increase detected by day 32 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A further increase in serum affinity after E2 boost was detected by day 32.
source: A modest but significant increase in serum affinity, however, was detected by day 17, with a further increase detected by day 32 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A relatively small portion of serum IgG underwent affinity maturation by day 17 in response to the E2 boost.
source: We interpret this to mean that a relatively small portion of serum IgG underwent affinity maturation by day 17 in response to the E2 boost and was not detectable by the Urea avidity assay due to high variability and the high pre-existing IgG titres (Figure 1E), or other limitations of the Urea assay (Alexander et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: Boosting with the E4 variant elicited slower increases in relative affinity and avidity, only detectable by day 32.
source: Boosting with the E4 variant elicited slower increases in relative affinity and avidity, only detectable by day 32, but by then representing an equivalent, if not greater, increase compared to that induced by E2 (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: By day 32, the increase in affinity and avidity after E4 boost was equivalent, if not greater, compared to that induced by E2.
source: Boosting with the E4 variant elicited slower increases in relative affinity and avidity, only detectable by day 32, but by then representing an equivalent, if not greater, increase compared to that induced by E2 (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: Memory T-cells are necessary for memory B-cell responses against haptens and viral proteins (Aiba et al., 2010; Hebeis et al., 2004).
source: Memory T-cells are necessary for memory B-cell responses against haptens and viral proteins (Aiba et al., 2010; Hebeis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aiba et al., 2010; Hebeis et al., 2004.

claim: There was no evidence that the memory T-cell response to re-stimulation by variant E-proteins was any different from re-stimulation by E3.
source: We found no evidence that the memory T-cell response to re-stimulation by variant E-proteins was any different from re-stimulation by E3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A deficiency in T-cell recognition of variant E-proteins cannot explain the differences in response to E2 and E4 challenge.
source: These data imply that a deficiency in T-cell recognition of these antigens cannot explain the differences in response to E2 and E4 challenge, and supports the idea that either T-cell receptors can recognize antigenic peptides from regions with around 50% sequence difference (see discussion) or, more likely, B-cells present peptides from different, more conserved regions than those their antibodies bind to.
evidence: This is an inference based on the T-cell proliferation data.

claim: Serum levels of anti-E4 IgG rose to a moderate level by day 17 after E4 priming.
source: Serum levels of anti-E4 IgG rose to a moderate level by day 17 (mean EPT = 3.6, Figure 4A), being less than seen after E4 boosting (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anti-E4 IgG levels after E4 priming were less than seen after E4 boosting.
source: Serum levels of anti-E4 IgG rose to a moderate level by day 17 (mean EPT = 3.6, Figure 4A), being less than seen after E4 boosting (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figures 4A and 1F.

claim: GC B-cell levels rose to a mean of 0.8% lymphocytes at day 7 after E4 priming.
source: GC B-cell levels rose to a mean of 0.8% lymphocytes at day 7 after E4 priming, half as much as after the E4 boost, then fell similarly to the post boost samples by around 60% by day 17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GC B-cell levels at day 7 after E4 priming were half as much as after the E4 boost.
source: GC B-cell levels rose to a mean of 0.8% lymphocytes at day 7 after E4 priming, half as much as after the E4 boost, then fell similarly to the post boost samples by around 60% by day 17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 4B and Figure 2B.

claim: GC B-cell levels after E4 priming fell by around 60% by day 17.
source: GC B-cell levels rose to a mean of 0.8% lymphocytes at day 7 after E4 priming, half as much as after the E4 boost, then fell similarly to the post boost samples by around 60% by day 17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells fell over time after E4 priming.
source: As with the E-boost GCs, the proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells fell over time (Figure 4C) and levels of VH mutation in all B-cells and IgM+ B cells increased (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Levels of VH mutation in all B-cells increased over time after E4 priming.
source: As with the E-boost GCs, the proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells fell over time (Figure 4C) and levels of VH mutation in all B-cells and IgM+ B cells increased (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Levels of VH mutation in IgM+ B cells increased over time after E4 priming.
source: As with the E-boost GCs, the proportion of IgM+ GC B-cells fell over time (Figure 4C) and levels of VH mutation in all B-cells and IgM+ B cells increased (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The median level of VH mutation in IgM+ GC B-cells at day 7 after E4 priming is less (=2) than after E4 boosting (=3).
source: The median level of VH mutation in IgM+ GC B-cells at day 7 after E4 priming is less (=2) than after E4 boosting (=3) suggesting, not conclusively, that GC Bells at day 7 after E4 boosting are memory derived.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The lower median VH mutation in IgM+ GC B-cells after E4 priming compared to E4 boosting suggests that GC B-cells at day 7 after E4 boosting are memory derived.
source: The median level of VH mutation in IgM+ GC B-cells at day 7 after E4 priming is less (=2) than after E4 boosting (=3) suggesting, not conclusively, that GC Bells at day 7 after E4 boosting are memory derived.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of mutation levels.

claim: No 7M Urea-resistant IgG was detected 7 or 17 days after E4 priming.
source: Antibody titres were insufficient to do a relative affinity competition ELISA and no 7M Urea-resistant IgG was detected 7 or 17 days after E4 priming (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental results.

claim: 48 recombinant antibodies (rAbs) were made, 38 of which were IgM.
source: We made 48 recombinant antibodies (rAbs), 38 of which were IgM (supplementary file 2), 24 from E4 primed mice (day 7 and day 17) and 24 from E4 boosted mice (day 7).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: 24 rAbs were made from E4 primed mice (day 7 and day 17).
source: We made 48 recombinant antibodies (rAbs), 38 of which were IgM (supplementary file 2), 24 from E4 primed mice (day 7 and day 17) and 24 from E4 boosted mice (day 7).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: 24 rAbs were made from E4 boosted mice (day 7).
source: We made 48 recombinant antibodies (rAbs), 38 of which were IgM (supplementary file 2), 24 from E4 primed mice (day 7 and day 17) and 24 from E4 boosted mice (day 7).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: The efficiency of detection of positive binding rAbs was quite low but consistent with the 30–50% binding frequency of GC rAbs previously observed (Kuraoka et al., 2016).
source: Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2, show the results from the initial screen of all rAbs against E4, indicating that the efficiency of detection of positive binding (deemed as O.D. > 0.1, useful for subsequent titration) was quite low but consistent with the 30–50% binding frequency of GC rAbs previously observed (Kuraoka et al., 2016), except for E4 prime day 7, which has only 2/13 rAbs binding strongly enough to be titrated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuraoka et al., 2016 and experimental data in Figure 4F.

claim: E4 prime day 7 had only 2/13 rAbs binding strongly enough to be titrated.
source: Figure 4F and Supplementary file 2, show the results from the initial screen of all rAbs against E4, indicating that the efficiency of detection of positive binding (deemed as O.D. > 0.1, useful for subsequent titration) was quite low but consistent with the 30–50% binding frequency of GC rAbs previously observed (Kuraoka et al., 2016), except for E4 prime day 7, which has only 2/13 rAbs binding strongly enough to be titrated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Low binding efficiency of E4 prime day 7 rAbs might be expected of antibodies from a day 7 primary response GC, indicating they were overall of lower affinity.
source: This might be expected of antibodies from a day 7 primary response GC, and indicated they were overall of lower affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected characteristics of primary response antibodies.

claim: All but one of the positive binding rAbs were IgM.
source: All but one of the positive binding rAbs were IgM.
